carousels.title: I automated 6 hours of work. Here's how.
slides: Finance teams spend 80% of their time collecting data. Not analyzing it.
Six hours of manual key-in every month. 15 KPIs. 17 countries.
Advanced Excel formulas now calculate everything. Copilot helped write them.
Five minutes to update the whole sheet. Colour codes itself automatically.
The formula that replaced 6 hours is two lines long.

carousels.title: It used to take 2 weeks. Now it takes 5 minutes.
slides: Most reports are outdated before they reach the person who needs them.
Manual extraction means the data is always from last Tuesday.
A live pipeline pulls directly from the source. The report stays current.
SAP to Tableau Prep to Tableau Desktop. Five minutes. Always today's data.
Static reports are a symptom. The pipeline is the fix.

carousels.title: I stopped doing it manually. Here's what I built instead.
slides: 62% of work time goes to tasks that repeat. Most never get automated.
The assumption is that fixing it requires coding. It does not.
Describe the repetition. Build one solution. It replaces the task permanently.
42 hours recurring. Built one Excel VBA + OCR tool. Two minutes every time after that.
Find the repeat. That is the only thing standing between you and the fix.

carousels.title: The report nobody wanted to write. Now it writes itself.
slides: The average professional spends 2.6 hours every day on writing tasks. McKinsey.
Most of it is the same type of writing with slightly different content each time.
A template and an AI first draft handle the repetition. You handle the judgment.
Draft in under 3 minutes. Review it. Adjust it. Send it. The 2.6 hours becomes 30 minutes.
Stop writing from scratch. The blank page is the most expensive part.

carousels.title: One weekend of setup. Zero effort every week after.
slides: The average employee spends 50 days a year on recurring manual tasks.
The task is not the problem. The absence of a system around it is.
One system converts every week into never again.
One weekend to build. Every week after: nothing. The system runs.
What keeps coming back is exactly what should be automated first.

carousels.title: The task I hated most. I never think about it now.
slides: 64% of employees with Microsoft Copilot access never open it.
It is already on the company laptop. Installed. Waiting. Unused.
One real use case is all it takes to change the habit completely.
Excel formulas. Email drafts. Meeting summaries. All handled inside the tools already there.
Open Copilot. Type one task done every week. See what changes.

carousels.title: I used to dread this. Then I built a system.
slides: The average worker switches between 10 apps 25 times every day.
Every context switch costs 23 minutes of focus to fully recover.
One connected system removes the switching entirely.
Data moves automatically between tools. No tab switching. No copy-pasting. No lost focus.
Count every app switch made tomorrow. That number shows exactly where the system goes.

carousels.title: 9 months of failure. 1 week. Same result.
slides: Most projects fail not because of the tool chosen. Because of the starting point.
Building the dashboard before the data is clean always ends the same way.
Tableau Prep first. Clean and structure the data before building anything.
Nine months of failure. Changed the starting point. Twenty-five templates delivered in one week.
The right order matters more than the right tool.

carousels.title: The AI tool I use every single day.
slides: One tool opens first every single morning. Before email. Before anything else.
Research that used to take an hour: under five minutes.
The gap between AI-assisted work and manual work is widening every month.
Claude handles research, structure, and drafts. The judgment and final decisions stay mine.
Pick one task repeated every week. Run it through Claude today. See what changes.

carousels.title: Claude just replaced 3 hours of my week.
slides: Three hours of the week disappeared. The actual work did not.
Newsletter research and drafting used to take hours. Now it takes a 10-minute review.
Claude researches the topic, writes the structure, drafts every section.
Read it. Adjust the tone. Approve it. Done.
The human part is judgment. Everything else is handled.

carousels.title: Nobody tells you this about Tableau Prep.
slides: Most people go straight to Tableau Desktop. That is the wrong starting point.
Tableau Prep is the step before the dashboard. Data cleaning, transformation, shaping.
Raw data from SAP goes in. Clean, structured data comes out. Automatically.
Change one thing in Prep and every downstream report updates. No manual retouch needed.
The dashboard takes minutes when the data pipeline is already clean.

carousels.title: This tool turns rough notes into a finished deck.
slides: Every important meeting leaves behind rough notes. Every presentation starts with a blank slide.
Paste those notes into Gamma. Describe the structure needed.
Three minutes: full slide deck. Layout, content, structure all generated.
Edit the slides that need adjustment. The first draft is already there to work from.
The two hours was always the blank page problem. This removes the blank page.

carousels.title: How GitHub Actions runs my work while I sleep.
slides: Every Monday at 1am a newsletter sends to the subscriber list. Asleep when it happens.
GitHub Actions checks a YAML schedule and triggers a Python script automatically.
Claude researches and drafts. The script formats and sends. Delivered before morning.
The schedule was set once. It has fired every single week since without any intervention.
Any task that repeats on a schedule can be handed to GitHub Actions the same way.

carousels.title: Perplexity changed how I do research. Here's why.
slides: Research used to mean 15 open tabs, two hours, and a messy document of copied quotes.
Perplexity reads the sources and returns a synthesized answer with citations.
Every citation links to the original source. Verifiable. Not hallucinated.
Used before every meeting that needs preparation and every report that needs external context.
One prompt. Five minutes. Research done. Check the sources and move on.

carousels.title: Power BI vs Tableau. Honest take after using both.
slides: Power BI and Tableau both do dashboards. The difference is where your data lives.
Power BI integrates natively with the Microsoft stack: Excel, SharePoint, Teams, Fabric.
Tableau wins on visual flexibility, Tableau Prep pipelines, and mixed data source connections.
Microsoft-heavy company: Power BI. Mixed or SAP-heavy data: Tableau.
Pick based on the actual data stack. The tool that fits the data is the right one.

carousels.title: The free tool that automates my most hated task.
slides: Power Automate comes free with every Microsoft 365 subscription. Almost nobody uses it.
It connects apps, triggers on events, and runs flows without a single line of code.
A file lands in SharePoint: the flow runs, sends a summary, updates a sheet automatically.
Zero extra cost. Runs in the background. No developer needed.
Open Power Automate today. It is already sitting in the Microsoft account.

carousels.title: This is the only AI I actually trust at work.
slides: At work, data belongs inside the company network. Not every AI meets that standard.
Microsoft Copilot is built into the company laptop and meets enterprise data requirements.
It drafts emails in Outlook, writes Excel formulas, and summarizes meetings in Teams.
Tested several AI tools. One is safe to use with real company data. That is Copilot.
For work tasks with real company data: Copilot. For personal projects: Claude.

carousels.title: Excel still wins. But only for this.
slides: People keep saying Excel is dead. It is not. It is just being used wrong.
For formulas, logic, and conditional calculations across complex conditions: still unmatched.
For dashboards, automated pipelines, and live data: better tools exist now.
Know which job each tool is built for. Use the right one for each.
Use Copilot to write the formulas directly inside Excel. That part has changed completely.

carousels.title: The exact prompt I use to summarise any report.
slides: Every KPI report has ten pages. Three things actually matter to the person reading it.
Finding those three things used to take 30 minutes of reading and re-reading.
Paste the report. Add: "Summarise this in three bullets. Each under 20 words."
The three most important points out in under 2 minutes. Ready to send.
The longer the report, the more this saves. Try it on the next one received.

carousels.title: Copy this prompt. Save 2 hours.
slides: Writing management summaries from raw data used to take most of a morning.
The data was right there. The writing was the entire bottleneck.
Prompt: "Here is the data. Write a management summary. 200 words. Highlight what changed vs last month."
First draft in under 3 minutes. Review it. Adjust it. Send it. Morning reclaimed.
The writing part of reporting is now the fastest part.

carousels.title: 5 prompts I use every week. Save this.
slides: Prompt 1: "Summarise this in 3 bullets under 20 words each."
Prompt 2: "Turn these notes into action items, decisions, and open questions."
Prompt 3: "Write a first draft of this email in under 100 words. Professional tone."
Prompt 4: "Build an Excel formula that [describe the logic]. Explain how it works."
Prompt 5: "Check this for errors, gaps, and anything that sounds unclear."

carousels.title: The Claude prompt that replaces Google for research.
slides: Google returns links. Every one of them still needs to be read manually.
Claude returns a synthesized answer when given enough context to work with.
The difference is specificity. A vague question gets a vague answer every time.
Format: "I am a [role]. I need to understand [topic]. Explain clearly in [format]."
Add the role and what the research is for. The answer becomes immediately usable.

carousels.title: Ask AI to build your Excel formula. Use this prompt.
slides: Writing Excel formulas from memory is a skill. Asking AI to write them is faster.
Describe what the formula needs to do in plain English. Claude or Copilot writes it.
Prompt: "Write an Excel formula that [logic]. Data is in [column range]."
Paste the formula. Test it. If it breaks, paste the error back. It fixes itself.
Copilot in Excel does this directly inside the spreadsheet. No copy-pasting required.

carousels.title: My notes were a mess. This prompt fixed that.
slides: Meeting notes that only made sense for the two hours after the meeting.
Action items buried in paragraphs. Decisions not separated from discussions.
Paste the raw notes. Add: "Pull out all action items, decisions, and open questions."
Clean structured output in under 30 seconds. Share it directly with the team.
The notes do not need to be clean for this to work. Rough input gives clean output.

carousels.title: Ask Claude this. Get a finished first draft.
slides: The blank page is the most expensive part of any writing task.
A first draft removes the blank page. Editing is always faster than starting from zero.
Never ask for the final version. Ask for a first draft with specific constraints.
Give it: who is reading this, what they need to know, how long, and what tone.
The gap between what Claude produces and what gets sent is usually 10 minutes of editing.

carousels.title: The prompt I run every Monday morning.
slides: Every Monday starts the same way. One prompt. Five minutes. The week is organized.
Prompt: "Here are this week's tasks: [list]. Rank by urgency and impact. Suggest a day for each."
Output: a prioritized weekly plan built in under 5 minutes.
The week starts with clarity instead of 30 minutes of deciding what to do first.
Paste the task list into Claude every Monday. The planning handles itself.

carousels.title: How to get AI to check your own work.
slides: Checking your own work misses the errors already believed to be correct.
AI has no assumptions about what was intended. It reads exactly what is written.
Paste the work. Add: "Find errors, unclear points, and anything that could be misread."
Read every flag. Fix what is genuinely wrong. Ignore what it misunderstands.
Use it before anything goes to a manager, client, or stakeholder. Not after.

carousels.title: One prompt. One hour saved. Every single time.
slides: One hour per week. Same task. Every single week.
52 hours a year. That is 6.5 full working days on one repeating task.
One well-written prompt completes it in under 10 minutes.
Writing the prompt once takes 15 minutes. The savings start immediately after.
Calculate how many times this task runs per year. That is how much is about to be reclaimed.

carousels.title: How I send a newsletter every week without writing it.
slides: Every Monday at 1am a newsletter sends to the subscriber list. Written by AI.
Claude researches the topic from RSS feeds and Reddit. Drafts the full content.
GitHub Actions runs the schedule. Triggers the Python script. Sends via Gmail API.
Built over one weekend. Has run automatically every week since without any changes.
Three parts: a research agent, a writing pipeline, and a scheduled delivery trigger.

carousels.title: The 3-step pipeline behind my monthly reports.
slides: Monthly reports used to take most of a week. The same three steps manually every time.
Step 1: Extract data from SAP Fiori. Raw, unformatted, directly from the source system.
Step 2: Tableau Prep runs the cleaning flow. Structured, consistent, ready data out.
Step 3: Tableau Desktop reads the Prep output. Live dashboard. Always current.
Three steps. One pipeline. A week of work is now five minutes.

carousels.title: I built an automation that works while I sleep.
slides: Sunday night. Nothing running manually. Monday morning: newsletter delivered.
GitHub Actions checks the YAML schedule. Fires at the time set once months ago.
Python script calls the Claude API. Formats the output. Sends via Gmail. Done.
No manual step at any point. The system decides when to run and runs it.
Any task that happens on a schedule can be handed off this exact way.

carousels.title: Every tool in my work stack. And exactly why.
slides: Seven tools. Each does exactly one thing. Nothing overlaps.
Claude for personal research and drafting. Microsoft Copilot for work tasks with company data.
Tableau Prep for data cleaning. Tableau Desktop for reporting and dashboards.
SAP Fiori for source data extraction. GitHub Actions for scheduling. Python for scripting.
Add a tool only when something genuinely cannot be done without it.

carousels.title: How I built a dashboard that updates itself.
slides: A dashboard that needs a manual refresh every Monday is not a real dashboard.
Connect Tableau Desktop directly to a Tableau Prep flow as the data source.
Tableau Prep runs on schedule. Pulls from SAP Fiori. Cleans and structures the output.
Every time Tableau Desktop opens, the latest cleaned data is already there.
The pipeline runs itself. The dashboard is always current. No Monday prep needed.

carousels.title: Built it once on a Saturday. Still running.
slides: Saturday afternoon. Four hours. One newsletter pipeline built from scratch.
Configured the GitHub Actions YAML. Wrote the Python script. Connected the Claude API.
Tested twice. Fixed one API error. Third run worked. Left it running.
Has fired automatically every Monday since. Never needed to touch it again.
The four hours paid back in the first week. Every week after is free.

carousels.title: How to connect live data to a Tableau report.
slides: Static reports go stale the moment they stop being updated. Live reports do not.
Step 1: Build a Tableau Prep flow that pulls from the source and cleans the data.
Step 2: In Tableau Desktop, set the data source to the Prep output, not the raw file.
Step 3: Schedule the Prep flow. Every refresh pulls the latest data automatically.
The only manual step is opening Tableau Desktop. Everything else is already done.

carousels.title: The blueprint for my most-used automation.
slides: Every automation built follows the same three-part structure. No exceptions.
Part 1: Trigger. Something fires it. A schedule, a file landing, a form submitted.
Part 2: Script. A Python file runs and does the actual work.
Part 3: Output. The result goes somewhere — email, file, sheet, or dashboard.
Trigger. Script. Output. Map any repeating task to those three parts and build it.

carousels.title: Here is the full stack. No gatekeeping.
slides: Full stack. Every tool used. No gatekeeping.
AI: Claude for personal work. Microsoft Copilot for anything using company data.
Data: SAP Fiori for extraction. Tableau Prep for cleaning. Tableau Desktop for reporting.
Automation: GitHub Actions for scheduling. Python for scripting. Gmail API for delivery.
Personal tools stay separate from company tools. That line matters and should not be crossed.

carousels.title: Start with this system. Build everything else later.
slides: One system before anything else. The most repeated task in the current workflow.
Write down every manual step in that task from start to finish.
Replace step one with a tool. Step two with a prompt. Step three with a trigger.
Test it. Fix what breaks. Leave everything else exactly as it is for now.
Build the second system only after the first one runs reliably on its own.

carousels.title: What AI still cannot do. From someone who tries daily.
slides: Three things AI consistently gets wrong no matter how good the prompt is.
First: judgment calls that need context only someone inside the situation has.
Second: reading the room. Knowing what a stakeholder needs to hear vs what is true.
Third: catching errors in data it was never told was wrong. It trusts the input completely.
Use AI for execution. Keep the judgment. The two are not interchangeable.

carousels.title: I used AI for everything for 30 days. Honest results.
slides: Thirty days. Every work task. AI first. No exceptions.
What improved: speed on first drafts, research depth, formula accuracy in Excel.
What got worse: writing from scratch without AI. The cold-start ability weakened.
What surprised me: how much time was going to tasks that could have been automated months earlier.
Use it deliberately. Not for everything. For the tasks where it is genuinely faster and better.

carousels.title: Stop using AI like a search engine.
slides: Most people open Claude the same way they open Google. Short question. Vague result.
AI is not a search engine. It is a thinking partner. The interaction is different.
Give it a role first: "You are a financial analyst preparing a monthly KPI report."
Give it context: what is being done, what good output looks like, what to avoid.
The quality of the output is entirely determined by the quality of the context provided.

carousels.title: The AI tool everyone recommends. My honest take.
slides: ChatGPT is the one everyone mentions first. Four weeks of daily use later: honest take.
Strong on general tasks and creative writing. Consistent when prompts are familiar.
Hallucinated facts on two verifiable research questions. Both answers sounded completely confident.
For tasks where accuracy matters, always verify the output against something real.
Right tool for the right task. ChatGPT for general use. Claude for research and reasoning.

carousels.title: What nobody tells you about automation.
slides: Automation breaks. Quietly. Often at the worst possible moment.
A script that worked 20 times will fail on run 21 when the data format shifts by one column.
Build a failure alert into every automation before anything else.
The newsletter pipeline ran silently broken for 5 weeks. No alert. No error. Just silence.
Build the check first. Build the automation second. That order matters.

carousels.title: AI made me worse at this one thing.
slides: AI made one specific skill weaker. Worth being honest about it.
Writing from scratch. Starting without a draft is harder than it was six months ago.
When a first draft is always one prompt away, the cold-start ability slowly declines.
Noticed this after using Claude for drafting consistently for three months straight.
Keep practicing both. Do not outsource the skill entirely. The judgment layer needs it.

carousels.title: When AI gives the wrong answer. And you trust it.
slides: The wrong answer delivered with confidence looks exactly like the right one.
AI does not know what it does not know. It answers with the same tone regardless.
Inside your domain, the errors are catchable. In an unfamiliar area, they are not.
The KPI formula AI wrote worked in 14 of 17 countries. Three had exceptions it missed.
Always test outputs against something real before trusting them in a work context.

carousels.title: The part of my job AI will never replace.
slides: One question at the end of every Friday: what here could only a person have done?
The answer is always the same. Stakeholder judgment. Context that lives in relationships.
Knowing the CFO prefers context before numbers. AI does not know that.
Knowing when a KPI that looks bad has a valid explanation. AI reads the number, not the situation.
Automate everything around that judgment. The judgment itself stays yours.

carousels.title: Never used Claude? Start here.
slides: First time opening Claude. Exact starting point.
Go to claude.ai. Type one task from this week that took longer than it should.
Add: "I work as a [role]. Here is what good output looks like: [describe it]."
Read the result. Edit what is wrong. That editing is where the skill builds.
Do this once today. Once tomorrow. The habit builds faster than expected.

carousels.title: Your first automation. 20 minutes. No code.
slides: First automation. 20 minutes. No code required at all.
Pick one task that repeats every week and never changes much.
Open Make.com. Free account. Connect two tools already in use.
Set a trigger on one event. Set the output to wherever the result needs to go.
Test it twice. Leave it running. First automation done.

carousels.title: The 3 AI tools you actually need. Not 30.
slides: Three tools. Not 30. These cover almost everything.
Claude: research, drafting, thinking through problems. Start here first.
Perplexity: research with citations. Use it when accuracy and sources matter.
Make.com or GitHub Actions: connect tools, run schedules, automate triggers.
Add a fourth only when the first three genuinely cannot cover the task.

carousels.title: How to use AI at work without looking like you depend on it.
slides: The fear: using AI makes it look like the work is not really yours.
Lead with the problem and the outcome. Never lead with which tool was used.
Nobody asks a surgeon which scalpel they used. They ask about the result.
The judgment, domain knowledge, and final decision: those are still entirely yours.
AI is a professional tool. Frame it that way and every impression follows from that.

carousels.title: You do not need to code to automate your job.
slides: Most useful automations at work require no code at all.
Power Automate, Make.com, and Zapier connect tools and run triggers without writing anything.
Describe the task in plain English to Claude. Ask it to explain how to automate it step by step.
Follow the steps. Connect the tools. Claude writes any code needed if it comes to that.
The only requirement is knowing what the task is and what the output should be.

carousels.title: Start with this. Everything else can wait.
slides: One task before anything else. The one that repeats every week without fail.
Write down every step of that task from opening the file to sending the output.
Automate step one. Not all of them. Just the first one.
Let it run for two weeks. See what breaks. Fix it. Then add step two.
The full automation comes from stacking small fixes, not from building everything at once.
